newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: SNB sticks to "generous" policy - Gehrig.
newsitem.headline: SNB sticks to "generous" policy - Gehrig.

text.p: continue its current monetary policy of controlled expansion, holding to a path between doing "too much" and "too little," SNB board member Bruno Gehrig said.
Gehrig, one of the SNB's three directors, said that inflationary fears were "scarcely justified" in Switzerland, according to the text of remarks prepared for delivery at an economic symposium.
Domestic credit demand was stagnant. Switzerland also had the largest industrial overcapacity, measured in terms of its "output gap", of all the OECD countries, he said.

"Against such a background, we will continue to set forth our controlled generous monetary policy, so that the central bank's central bank money supply aggregate likely will remain above the medium-term growth path," Gehrig said in the speech to the Economic Society of the Canton of Berne.
The SNB's current policy stance was necessary given the current weak state of the Swiss economy.
"The year 1997 will be another difficult one for the Swiss economy, but one with likely only scant inflation and hopefully with moderately positive growth," Gehrig said.

Swiss Gross Domestic Product in 1996 is expected to be slightly negative, showing a decline of about 0.5 percent, Swiss economists say. The SNB said last month that it expected growth to be around 0.5 percent in 1997.

The SNB said at its December news briefing that it would keep watch for any signs that inflation was on the rise again, but would meanwhile stick to an expansive policy until there were clear signs of an economic upturn.

The SNB's medium-term target for its central bank money aggregate M0 is one percent per year. M0, which had lagged below the target, rose above the target path in 1996, and is expected to show average growth of 4.5 percent in the fourth quarter 1996 versus the same 1995 quarter.
"Of course we will keep a critical watch on the development and necessary changes in our policy -- in whichever direction that may be -- will be ushered in at the appropriate time," Gehrig said.
With respect to the SNB's continued reliance on a monetary growth path target, Gehrig said the indicator was still useful.

"The growth path is nothing more and also nothing less than a medium-term orientation measure for what we do from quarter to quarter. It describes an ideal monetary path, which according to our knowledge and under the premise of normal capacity utilisation leads to price stability," Gehrig said.
"Its disciplinary effect lies not in the fact that we do not avoid deviations, but that we must explain and justify them," Gehrig said.
He also said, however, that it was not enough as a general rule to simply keep the aggregate on path in order to avoid inflation, and the same held true in order to avoid recession.
"No monetary policy concept is definitive and sacrosant. That also applies to the SNB's policy," Gehrig said.
